articles.headline: Additional Local.
articles.text: Johnny Goodall expects to start for New Orleans in a few days.
articles.summary: Johnny Goodall plans to leave for New Orleans.

articles.text: Bob Roberts and Vic. Smith will start for New Orleans Saturday or Sunday.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts and Vic. Smith will leave for New Orleans this weekend.

articles.text: The coach arrived at eight o'clock this morning, and started on the return trip at ten.
articles.summary: The stage coach arrived at eight and left again at ten.

articles.text: Tickets from Bismarck to New Orleans and return, good for forty-five days, are selling for $36.24.
articles.summary: Round-trip fare from Bismarck to New Orleans is $36.24.

articles.text: Count Rembielinski has returned to Paris, after a successful hunt with Vic. Smith. He will return next summer, and, in company with Vic., take a three-months' hunt in the Big Horn country. Vic. and the count together killed about two hundred and twenty-five deer and antelope within fifteen miles of Medora.
articles.summary: Count Rembielinski returned to Paris after hunting with Vic. Smith, who with him killed about 225 deer and antelope near Medora.

articles.text: Father Martin came Monday evening, and Tuesday morning made James and Julia Butler one. He says that the library books will be here Tuesday or Wednesday. They will be in charge of John O'Sullivan. Arrangements for drawing them are not made, but some simple plan will doubtless be adopted. Father Martin went to Glendive Tuesday evening.
articles.summary: Father Martin married James and Julia Butler and reported library books coming in John O'Sullivan's charge.

articles.text: C. F. Ellison is fast filling the ice houses with a first rate quality of ice. He has built a long track from the dam to the houses, and the ice is drawn upon these, thus making much faster time than by loading on wagons. About thirty men are employed putting up ice. In addition to the ice to be put in the houses, Mr. Ellison will put up a large quality to be stored in the cooling rooms of the company as soon as completed.
articles.summary: C. F. Ellison is filling the company ice houses using about thirty men and a track from the dam.

articles.text: Work at the coal mine has been brisk lately, and it is an undisputed fact that the quality is superior to anything yet found along the line. When mined the coal is almost as glossy as anthracite. It burns freely and gives out an intense heat. The great weight of the butte is doubtless the cause of its superior quality, shown by the fact that until the tunnel had pierced to a depth of eighty feet, well under the butte, the coal was only of ordinary quality, except for a twelve to thirty-six-inch strip at the bottom of the vein.
articles.summary: The Medora coal mine is producing superior coal from deep under the butte.

articles.text: We are glad to see the name of E. A. Henderson mentioned prominently for the position of clerk of the senate. Leaving the consideration aside that Mr. Henderson has occupied similar positions both in Minnesota and Dakota, which gives him abundant experience, his many good qualities and the service he has done the Republican party entitles him to the position. No other candidate has been mentioned prominently, and we earnestly hope that he will be the unanimous choice to the position for which he is so well fitted.
articles.summary: The paper backs E. A. Henderson for clerk of the territorial senate.

articles.text: The benefits of advertising are so apparent that it seems almost unnecessary to call attention to them. An illustration coming to our notice, however, deserves comment. William Miller, of Minnesela, lost some horses on Grand river, and as our readers know, advertised them in the COW BOY. Mr. Miller, after inserting the advertisement, went up and down the railroad and stage road and finally returned to Minnesela. He had hardly reached home before he received word from Mr. Becket, of Dickinson, to the effect that his horses were there, having been recognized from the description in the COW BOY. The end was not as pleasant, however. Mr. Miller return to Dickinson, and in company with Henry Turner, John H. Stevens and son Horace, started for the Hills. They reached the Cannon Ball late at night, and in attempting to cross, tipped over. They were so exhausted that they could not right the wagon and were forced to remain there till daylight. They then started for Springdale station, on the stage line, and arrived there in a badly frozen condition.
articles.summary: A Cow Boy ad helped William Miller recover strayed horses, but his party upset crossing the Cannon Ball and arrived at Springdale station badly frozen.

articles.headline: Married.
articles.text:
BUTLER—BUTLER—December 30, 188[1?], in the Catholic church at Medora, Dakota, by the Rev. Father Martin, James Butler and Julia Butler, both of Medora.

A change from the single to the married state almost invariably brings a change in name to the lady contracting, but in the above case, although no relationship existed, the name remained the same. This is the first wedding that has taken place in Medora, and the newly married couple are to be congratulated on the new departure. The bride and groom are both general favorites and enter upon their new relations with the heartiest good will of all. Mr. and Mrs. Butler will soon begin housekeeping at the Cantonment.
articles.summary: James Butler and Julia Butler married December 30 in Medora's Catholic church, the first wedding in Medora.

articles.text: From Little Missouri, July 6, 1884, a bay horse, eight years old and weighing about 1,000 pounds. The horse was branded with an anchor on left cheek and a hat brand on left shoulder. The above reward will be paid for the return of the following stock or a proportionate reward will be paid for the return of any of them. The stock consists of the following horses:

One bay mare, one brown mare and one roan mare, all young and branded double or reverse P on left shoulder as advertised in our brand columns. Also one light sorrel pony, white legs and face and branded NC on left shoulder and triangle JP on right shoulder also as advertised in our brand columns.

By the undersigned at Knutson creek sheep corrall, one mottled white and buckskin pony weighing about 850 pounds. Black nose and feet except the left hind foot, which is white. Also a dark bay pony weighing about 900 pounds, having white strip in forehead to end of nose. Brand is very indictinct on left hip but looks like G bar.

The owner or owners may recover same by calling on the undesigned, paying resonable charges and for the insertion of this notice.

articles.summary: Frank Walker has taken up two stray ponies at Knutson creek.

articles.text: The northern country is full of prospectors from the east and south looking for range locations and stock. There will not be much changing of ownership until spring, when a general stock boom is looked for. Quite a number are talking of stock contracts for spring delivery, and with all western and Texas cattle are the favorites, as they take to the range readily and commence rustling as soon as turned loose. Old-time Montana cattlemen think Idaho, Washington territory and Utah cattle cheaper at $35 per head than Texas stock at $20. Being natives of the country, they do well where imported animals die. They are also said to be better breeders, and the cows takes better care of their calves—[Stock Growers' Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped item on prospectors seeking ranges and stock for a spring boom.

articles.text: "Ex-Representative Upson, of Texas, is here as the legal representative of cattle raisers in the Southwest, for the purpose of securing the passage of a bill through Congress requiring the cattle trails of the West and South to be kept open. Within a few days he will be joined by others interested in this matter, and a strong effort will be made to procure the legislation. The complaint made is that the fencing in of enormous tracts of country in the West for grazing purposes has blocked the trail over which cattle are driven to eastern markets. In Indian Territory particularly, it is alleged, lately erected fences, inclosing the grazing lands leased from the Indians, extend across the cattle trails in different places. This will entail heavy loss upon the southwestern cattle raisers, unless Congress grants the relief asked, and compels the trails to be kept open.—[Nat. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped item on Texas cattle raisers' push to keep cattle trails open.

articles.text: Reports from up and down the Little Missouri river shows that the cattle are suffering somewhat from the protracted cold snap, but, the cattle owners do not anticipate anything serious, as there is plenty of grass and the cold snap will not continue much longer.
articles.summary: Cattle on the Little Missouri are suffering somewhat from the cold snap but owners expect no serious loss.

articles.text: A thoroughbred Kentucky heifer named Lillie Dale ate a leaf of tobacco and then lay down and gasped away $700 worth of blooded stock into the invisible beyond. By-and-by fine bred cattle will learn to leave the food of god-like man alone. Next thing you know, the race horse will get to drinking whiskey with the jockeys and a nice set of brutes we will have.—[The Review.
articles.summary: Clipped humor item about a heifer killed by eating tobacco.

articles.text: At a meeting of the Utah and Idaho Stock Growers' association, held at Ogden, on the 2d inst., among others the following resolutions were adopted, concerning the foolish habit of constantly carrying pistols where no necessity could possibly be shown for their use: Whereas, the custom of carrying fire-arms by those engaged in the round-up and in working in the cattle ranges is productive of great evil and frequently results in the damage of persons and property; be it therefore resolved, that the custom of carrying firearms, except in the immediate vicinity of Indian reservations, should be discountenanced, and it is hereby made the duty of members of this association, foremen of round-ups, and foremen of ranges, to use every effort in their power to prevent the carrying of firearms by cattlemen at times and places, except when absolutely necessary, and that the members of this association pledge themselves so far as in their power to carry out the spirit of this resolution.—[New Mexico Stock Grower.
articles.summary: Utah and Idaho stockmen resolve against carrying firearms on the range.

articles.text: One scarcely ever turns to an American paper, says a foreign cotemporary, but he comes on a discussion on the natural gait of the horse, the writers contending according to their opinions for pacing, trotting and galloping. Into this hop, step and jump of horse movements we do not care to enter, but we know that we have bred gallopers in the line of galloping for years, being determined that their ancestors could gallop, or, which is all the same, had a predisposition for galloping. The Americans have arrived at equally successful results. All of the paces are, however, natural, and there can be as much improvement made in either as in the formation of the animal when looked at from a stand-still showyard point of view. The old horse that could walk a mile and gallop a mile, is no more wanted now than the old groom who would advertise for a situation guaranteeing his ability to weed a garden, milk a cow, wait at table or drive a gig. We may have developed natural gaits, but we cannot say that any particular breed of horses, or horse as a whole, had one natural gait.
articles.summary: Clipped essay on the natural gaits of horses.

articles.text: A Washington dispatch says: The investigation of Indian land leases will be given over to a committee of senators with authority to visit all the reservations where the cattlemen have gained a foothold. This will make a summer's work, which will not be unpleasant and it may be beneficial to the health of the senators and the exchequers of the Indians. The senate committee on Indian affairs have held one meeting on the subject, and there was a disposition on the part of some members to defer the investigation until next summer, on the ground that the present session is so short and there is so much to attend to the senators could not give time to the inquiry without neglecting other duties. Others of the committee insisted on prosecuting the inquiry without delay. Senator Vest appeared before the committee and submitted the basis of his charges and a list of witnesses by whom the fraud in procuring the leases, he said, could be proved. A resolution calling upon the secretary of the interior for a detailed statement of the leases, the acreage so occupied, prices paid, etc., was adopted. Secretary Teller will not reply to this for a fortnight or more.—[River Press.
articles.summary: Senate investigation of cattlemen's Indian land leases.

articles.text: The live stock quarters at the New Orleans exposition are unusually ample, and are situated in the northwestern portion of the park, towards St. Charles avenue. There are six distinct buildings for horses and two for cattle, with stall room for 1,000 horses and 500 cattle. The buildings for horses will be the two parallel rows indicated on the plan of the grounds. Each will be 368 feet long by 60 feet wide and 24 feet high, and have stalls on either side, permitting the heads of the animals to face outward, thereby leaving a broad passage way through the middle of the building. The buildings for the cattle stand at either end of the buildings mentioned and at right angles with them. They are 378 feet long by 72 feet wide and 21 feet high. In addition to the structures for live stock, a regulation half-mile track is laid out adjoining the line of buildings. The track and space enclosed will also be used as an area for the display of live stock. These areas combined contain 2,080x780 feet, the stock exhibition covering 37 acres of ground. Over $125,000 has been appropriated by the management for premiums and the necessary expenses of making the live stock display. This is by far a larger sum than has ever before been devoted to a similar enterprise. The object of the management in making this princely grant of money is to secure the presence of the best examples of all classes of live stock to be found on this continent.—[N. W. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Live stock quarters at the New Orleans exposition.

articles.text: The pleasures of Christmas were not by any means forgotten in Medora, and our turkey engagement on that day at Rassie Deffebach's will be a long time sinking into forgetfulness.
articles.summary: The paper enjoyed Christmas turkey at Rassie Deffebach's.

articles.text: The dance at Roberts & Co.'s. hall Christmas eve was all that heart could wish. These dances are fast increasing in popularity, and well they may, as the management is strict in not allowing anything objectionable to mar their pleasure.
articles.summary: The Christmas eve dance at Roberts & Co.'s hall was a success.

articles.text: Some despicable villain put a bundle of lighted hay between the buildings occupied by Gill Kennedy and E. Elmer, Christmas morning. It may have been done as a joke, but it would have been a choke if the perpetrator had been discovered.
articles.summary: Someone set lighted hay between Gill Kennedy's and E. Elmer's buildings on Christmas morning.

articles.text: The Gladstone Express is the newest aspirant for journalistic honors and comes to us neatly printed and well edited. It is a rather forbidding time of the year to begin such an enterprise, but there is understood to be good backing behind the Express, and we hope it will succeed.
articles.summary: The new Gladstone Express newspaper is welcomed.

articles.text: "Ole" Anderson has left us. As a lightning jerker and jolly good fellow he has not a superior on the line. His change, taking Mr. Kelly's place as operator, at Dickinson, is a promotion, but it was as distasteful to him as to the many friends he left behind. Come again, Ole.
articles.summary: Telegraph operator "Ole" Anderson has left for Dickinson.

articles.text: The invincible didn't exactly meet the immovable, but the N. P. and Wells, Fargo express companies did in the persons of their respective route agents on this division, Messrs. DeForce and Heath Scripturally, "Great was the meet thereof." The last seen of them they were arm in arm, steering for the depot and conversing in confidential whispers that could have been heard at Sentinel Butte. The air in the Bad Lands is exceedingly bracing.
articles.summary: Express route agents DeForce and Heath met in Medora.

articles.text: We do not think there is a person in Medora but that regretted to see C. W. Sleeper depart Sunday morning. He has made a host of friends while in the employment of the N. P. R. C. Co. Mr. Sleeper's plans are as yet undecided, but it is his intention, if possible, to get hold of a bunch of cattle and start a ranch in the Bad Lands. William Van Driesche takes Mr. Sleeper's place as vice president, a choice that if the change had to be made, is more popular than that of any other man.
articles.summary: C. W. Sleeper left the N. P. R. C. Co.; William Van Driesche succeeds him as vice president.

articles.text: Mrs. L. A. Anderson, now of Glendive, writes the COW BOY regarding her domestic troubles. She claims Mr. Anderson abused her in a shameful manner, and that he is indebted to her and her son for work. She also states that he has women on the brain, and that two or more wives are not sufficient for him. According to her statement Mr. Anderson is on the verge of insanity. We hope this difficulty will be amicably settled before long, and that the parties interested will carry on their warfare in a less public manner. Newspaper airing of domestic troubles does not help either party, and causes any amount of gossip.
articles.summary: Mrs. L. A. Anderson of Glendive wrote the paper about her domestic troubles.

articles.text: George Roderick returned yesterday from Jamestown, whence he had driven overland. He made the trip in fifteen days, being delayed by blizzards and cold weather. The report reached here ahead of him that his feet were badly frozen crossing the Missouri, but it was false, only his nose and chin being tapped by Jack Frost. The man George was working for failed, and his time is a dead loss. He is too much of a rustler, however, to be discouraged, and is already on the alert for work. He left McNeave Nally in Jamestown, and brought back Jack Cameron in charge of his outfit.
articles.summary: George Roderick returned after a fifteen-day overland drive from Jamestown.

articles.text: About every so often, papers in the outside towns contain articles to the effect that Bob Roberts is shot. Papers are now stating this as a fact concerning our Bob Roberts, when he is as alive and hearty as ever. The Bob Roberts shot is a cow boy living near Miles City. A man named Sullivan shot him at a dance and then skipped. He was followed by the sheriff and a posse and trailed to a house a short distance from Miles. The sheriff ordered the family to come out, and as they were complying Sullivan shot the man and an infant child, and again got away from his pursuers. He was again followed and toward morning was found in a clump of bushes, without ammunition and nearly frozen.
articles.summary: Reports of Bob Roberts' shooting refer to a cowboy near Miles City, not Medora's Bob Roberts.
